content: The World Values Survey (WVS) is an ongoing academic initiative conducted by social scientists to evaluate sociocultural, moral, religious, and political values across various cultures globally. The findings of this project are largely accessible on its official website. The WVS originated from the European Values Study (EVS) in 1981, when the methodologies of the successful European study were extended to 14 countries outside Europe. However, the 1981 study only included 22 countries worldwide. The EVS was conducted under the leadership of Jan Kerkhofs and Ruud de Moor and remains based in the Netherlands at Tilburg University. Ronald Inglehart, from the University of Michigan in the United States, played a pivotal role in the early global expansion of the survey. The survey was repeated approximately every 10 years, forming what came to be known as waves. One of the project's objectives became the longitudinal and cross-cultural measurement of value variations. Subsequent waves followed at intervals of about five years. Due to its European origins, the early waves of the WVS had a Eurocentric focus, with limited representation in Africa and Southeast Asia. To address this, the WVS adopted a decentralized structure, allowing academic representatives from new countries to join a quasi-democratic network. New participants were required to conduct the predefined survey in their country with at least 1,000 interviewees. In return, they could exchange their data for access to the broader WVS dataset. Funding was primarily local, with representatives in each country financing their portion of the project. This decentralized approach allowed the WVS to expand beyond its Eurocentric roots, encompassing 42 countries in the second wave, 54 in the third wave, and 62 in the fourth wave. Today, the WVS database is freely accessible online. The WVS Secretariat is based in Sweden, while its official archive is located in Madrid, Spain. The WVS methodology involves administering detailed questionnaires through face-to-face interviews. Questionnaires from all five waves, including the incomplete 2005/2006 wave, are available in full on the WVS website. Recent questionnaires have included approximately 250 questions. In each country, these are administered to 1,000 to 3,500 interviewees, with an average of about 1,330 interviews per country in the fourth wave, totaling approximately 92,000 interviews worldwide. It is important to note that sampling methods vary between countries, leading to differences in results. For example, Slovenian social scientist Adam has highlighted significant discrepancies between the European Values Study 2001 (which aggregates European country studies from the WVS) and the European Social Survey 2002/2003. The WVS questionnaire consists of around 250 questions, resulting in 400 to 800 measurable variables. Some notable findings include: Happiness: Perceptions of happiness were measured, and this aspect of the WVS is widely cited in the media. The popular statistics website Nationmaster publishes a simplified world happiness scale derived from WVS data. The WVS website allows for more sophisticated analyses, such as tracking happiness over time or across socioeconomic groups. One striking finding was the significant drop in happiness among Russians and some other Eastern European countries during the 1990s. The Inglehart Map: This is one of the most well-known results of the WVS. Various variables were condensed into two dimensions of cultural variation: traditional vs. secular-rational and survival vs. self-expression. Based on these dimensions, countries were mapped into specific cultural regions. The WVS claims that these two dimensions explain over 70% of the cross-national variance in a factor analysis of ten indicators. Trust and Democracy: The survey found that trust and democracy are values that transcend most cultural boundaries. It also revealed that gender equality is one of the most significant differences between Western and other cultures. The WVS has inspired a range of literature. Dutch intercultural researcher Geert Hofstede has positively received research based on WVS findings. Specifically, Hofstede has noted that Inglehart's two-dimensional reduction of results, as represented by the Inglehart Map, supports his own work. For instance, Inglehart's well-being vs. survival dimension strongly correlates with Hofstede's dimensions of individualism and masculinity, while secular-rational vs. traditional authority correlates negatively with Hofstede's power distance dimension. However, Inglehart's two dimensions are not identical to Hofstede's five dimensions. Given the differences in methodology—Hofstede's research was based on work value surveys administered to IBM employees—it is unsurprising that there are differences between his results and those of the WVS.
